In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the anti-HBc test might be helpful in the reduction of false-negative donations in the blood supply from new donors, but that the test cannot be used as a general screening tool to exclude false-negative donations from the supply of regular donors, since it might ultimately result in the inclusion of false-negative donations.
the residual risk of transfusion-related HIV transmission in the Federal Republic of Germany is still very low, but not zero.

the introduction of anti-HBcscreening into routine blood donation procedures might result in a decrease of the residual HIV transmission risk, but that the magnitude of this reduction cannot be estimated from published data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
anti-HBc testing should not be used for the exclusion of HIV-seropositives from the blood supply, but that it should be used for the selection of donors who are at high risk of transmitting HBV.

, in spite of the fact that the anti-HBc test is a useful and important screening test for blood donations, its use in the screening of regular donors should be restricted to those countries where a high prevalence of HBV infection exists and/or where the prevalence of HIV infection is still high.

anti-HBc testing is a valuable tool for the reduction of the risk of transfusion-related HIV transmission, but only if the test is applied in conjunction with the exclusion of anti-HBcseropositive donations, and if the rate of anti-HBcvaccinated donors is low.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a sensitive and highly specific test for anti-HIV-1/2 and anti-HIV-2 is essential to ensure the safety of the blood supply.
the risk of transfusion-associated HIV infection is not eliminated by the use of anti-HIV antibody screening.

anti-HBc testing can be used as an additional tool to reduce the risk of transfusion-related HIV transmission, but it should not replace the current screening procedure for HIV and other blood-borne infections.
